title: AI credit scoring: how do lenders keep it fair and explainable?
description: Approve more good loans with an AI credit model you can explain: the tools, US and EU rules, three builds and our pick.
summary: AI credit scoring predicts whether an applicant will repay[^5]. When it says no, it must say why in plain words[^1][^35]. The model is the easy part; decline reasons[^33], bias checks[^31] and examiner paperwork[^7] make or break it.
humanRole: Chief credit officer: sets the score cutoffs and who may override them.[^49][^51] Examiners ask for every cutoff, the reason for it and each change.[^51]
Underwriter: decides the files between the approve and decline cutoffs, and any override.[^49][^52] Each override records the approving officer and the reason.[^49][^43]
Compliance officer: signs off the map from model drivers to decline reasons.[^33] Owns each decline letter: specific reasons that match what the model scored, within 30 days.[^1]
Model validator, independent of whoever built the model: checks it before first use.[^7] A small lender can hire an outside reviewer, but still owns the result.[^7][^40]
teamAfter: Underwriters work the hard files: the gray zone between cutoffs and the overrides.[^49] For simple consumer loans, BLS notes, underwriting may be fully automated.[^53]
Credit officers read a monthly override report: how many, why, who approved them and how those loans perform.[^49][^43]
Compliance checks overrides for fair lending. Examiners test declines above the cutoff and approvals below it separately for unequal treatment.[^50][^51]
Modelers watch whether the model still performs as products and borrowers change.[^7] When it drifts, they adjust or rebuild it.[^7]
verdict: Measure the payoff on your own loans, in dollars at your cutoff, not vendor claims[^17][^28].
Start with a scorecard: it gives the decline reasons US law requires[^1][^16].
Move to a complex model only if it beats the scorecard and your validators can check it[^7][^33].
Use AI to read loan documents, not to predict defaults; standard models predict better[^6][^13].
The software is free; the real cost is your team's time on data and decline reasons[^48][^33].

ownData.title: What are a lender's options for getting an AI credit model?
ownData.intro: Three ways lenders get a credit model, and what each leaves you owning. The price column comes from our check of six platforms on 26 November 2026[^22]. Whichever you pick, the decline reasons stay your job[^1][^40].

ownData.note: Experian's UK price leaves out build costs and add-ons[^23]. The other five platforms quote per contract[^17][^18][^19][^20][^21].

example.input: An application with income, debts and time at address, plus a credit bureau report pulled with consent.
example.output: A score and an approve or decline. For a decline, the top reasons in plain words, such as "debt is high compared with income", ready for the decline letter (adverse action notice).

recipes.name: 1. Small lender: explainable scorecard
recipes.when: Credit unions and community banks with a small analytics team, or an outside builder. The software is free[^46][^47], and the points table shows each decline reason directly[^16].
flow: IT: pull the application and credit bureau report
Modeler: group each input into ranges and give each range points (optbinning)
Modeler: add up the points into a score
Credit officer: set the cutoff and policy rules
Credit officer: run in shadow on one loan product beside today's decisions before it decides anything
Underwriter: review each decision and its top decline reasons
Compliance: one named person sends each decline letter
Modeler: check each quarter for accuracy drift and bias (fairlearn)
recipes.cost: Free open-source software[^46][^47]; the build is quoted per job, and after launch the cost is your team's review time. Our AI Sprint: $10,000, 30 days, fixed scope, with specs for 2 or 3 AI bets[^45].

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size lender: stronger model with plain-English reasons
recipes.when: Fintechs and regional lenders with a team that can validate the model before first use[^7].
flow: IT: pull application, bureau and bank-account data
IT: combine them into one table of inputs
Modeler: fit a stronger model that weighs many inputs at once (LightGBM)
Modeler: find which inputs drove each score (SHAP)
Modeler: turn those drivers into plain-English reasons
Compliance: sign off the reasons
Credit officer: set cutoffs in the decision engine
Credit officer: run in shadow on one loan product beside today's decisions before it decides anything
Compliance: one named person sends each decline letter
Modeler: check monthly against a simpler model that shows each input's effect (EBM)
recipes.cost: The model software can be open source, such as InterpretML's EBM[^48]. Cash-flow data and most decision platforms are quoted per contract[^25][^29][^18][^19]; of the platforms we checked, only Experian shows a public price[^22].

recipes.name: 3. Document-heavy files: AI reads, a normal model scores
recipes.when: Small business, mortgage and other files with many PDFs per application.
flow: IT: collect bank statements, pay stubs and tax returns
Modeler: have AI pull out the key fields
Underwriter: check each field the AI flags as shaky
Modeler: score with a scorecard or stronger model
Underwriter: review each decision and its reasons
Compliance: one named person sends each decline letter
recipes.cost: In our own benchmark, AI read fund reports of up to 57 pages for about $0.006 to $0.27 each, depending on the models[^34]. That was measured on fund reports, so benchmark it on your own loan files; see the AI document processing guide[^34].

tables.intro: Other teams' results on public data. AUC measures how well a model ranks repayers above defaulters: 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Your loan book can differ, which is why you benchmark.

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: A lender that declines an applicant must send a notice within 30 days, giving the specific reasons or how to ask for them[^1]. The reasons must match the factors the model actually scored[^1]. Every model needs a clean path to plain-English reasons, and one named person who sends each decline letter on time.

rules.name: Fair Credit Reporting Act, 15 U.S.C. 1681m(a)
rules.what: If a decline used a credit report and a credit score, the decline notice must also give that score[^38]. It must show the score's range, the key factors that hurt it (usually up to four), the date and who supplied it[^39]. Those key factors don't replace your own decline reasons[^1].

rules.name: CFPB circulars 2022-03 and 2023-03
rules.what: They said complex algorithms are no excuse for vague reasons[^35]. The guidance is gone; the rule it explained is not[^2][^1]. Don't read the withdrawal as a pass.

rules.name: Fed SR 26-2 and OCC Bulletin 2026-13, model risk guidance
rules.what: Banks of $30 billion or less in assets are generally excluded; where it applies, validate models before first use and document them[^3][^7]. Generative and agentic AI are out of scope[^7], and the OCC dropped its 1997 credit-scoring exam guide[^8]. Smaller lenders still answer for vendor models: outsourcing doesn't reduce a bank's or credit union's responsibility[^40][^42], and that has long covered bought models[^41].

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Scoring people's creditworthiness is high-risk; fraud detection is exempt[^4]. Lenders using it must assign trained human oversight and keep its logs[^11], and do a fundamental rights impact assessment[^12]. Plan now if you lend in the EU.

howToTest: Pick one loan product and record today's numbers first: approval rate, loss rate, time to decision and share of files reviewed by hand.
Take your booked loans with known outcomes. Hold out the latest loans old enough to show whether they repaid; that often takes 24 months or more[^43].
Booked loans can't show how the applicants you declined would have done[^44]. Modelers fill that gap with assumptions, a step called reject inference[^44].
Fit three models on the same data, inputs and split: a scorecard, an EBM and LightGBM. An EBM (Explainable Boosting Machine) shows each input's effect; LightGBM is stronger but harder to explain.
Compare AUC and KS on the held-out loans. Both measure how well a model separates repayers from defaulters; AUC runs from 0.5, a coin flip, to 1.0, perfect.
Turn each model's output into decline reasons, and check they stay the same when you refit on a new sample.
Price the lift in dollars at your cutoff: the extra approvals you gain and the losses you avoid. That tells you what a better model is worth.

Run a bias check with fairlearn or your own approval-gap analysis, across the groups fair-lending exams look at. For most non-mortgage loans, Regulation B bars asking applicants' race[^36], so estimate it with BISG, which infers race from surname and address[^37].
Pick the simplest model within a point or two of the best. Extra accuracy that you cannot explain costs more than it earns.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a platform when you have no modelling team, need a decision engine anyway, and are happy to use the vendor's models and data partners. Expect a quote, not a price list[^17][^18][^19].
buyVsBuild.build: Build when your own loan history is your edge. The main scorecard, explainable-model and bias-check software is free and open source[^46][^48][^47], and examiners judge any model by its validation and documentation[^7]. The work is data, validation and reason codes[^33].

watchOuts: A credit report's "key factors" list does not count as your decline reasons[^1]. Your model must produce its own[^1][^35].

SHAP shows which inputs drove a score, but it does not write Regulation B reasons, and some versions miss the true ones[^33][^5]. Group related inputs into a reason-code map that compliance signs off[^33].

Models trained on past lending data can carry past bias forward[^31][^32]. Check approval gaps before launch and every quarter, with BISG estimates where you can't ask race[^36][^37] and a tool such as fairlearn[^47].
Vendor lift numbers such as more approvals are measured on the vendor's chosen data[^17][^27][^28]. Ask for a benchmark on your own loans.

faq.q: Is it legal to use AI for credit decisions?
faq.a: Yes, under the same rules as any scoring model.[^1][^51] Each declined applicant gets specific reasons that match what the model scored.[^1] The OCC rates machine-learning scoring as the highest fair-lending risk.[^51]

faq.q: Is AI credit scoring more accurate than a scorecard?
faq.a: Sometimes, by a small margin.[^5] Boosted-tree models such as XGBoost lead on accuracy, but logistic regression holds up on small data.[^5] On LendingClub loans, LightGBM beat the best language model, 0.73 to 0.67 AUC.[^6]

faq.q: Can AI credit scoring be biased?
faq.a: Yes: models trained on past lending can carry past bias forward.[^31] Credit scores are already 5 to 10% less accurate for minority and low-income borrowers.[^32] Test approval gaps before launch and every quarter.[^47][^37]

faq.q: Do people still make the final call on a loan?
faq.a: Usually, yes. Few lenders let the score decide alone; files between two cutoffs get a manual review.[^49] In the EU, the people overseeing credit-scoring AI must be able to override it.[^52][^11]

BLS expects loan officer jobs to grow 1% from 2025 to 2035, with about 17,100 openings a year.[^53] Most lenders' software already recommends; loan officers review it and decide.[^53] Among US firms using AI, 66% use it only to help staff; 2% saw AI-related employment fall.[^54]

offer.heading: Not sure how to bring AI into credit decisions? Get a free diagnostic
offer.body: Tell us your loan products and how you score today. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step, a before-and-after measure and what your examiner will ask. You get it in writing, with no sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Couldn't see who decides what until the recipes. On this page now opens with who keeps the decision, follows the page order and links the FAQ. The recipe steps already name the role for each step.

Tripped on high-side and low-side overrides and on the reason-code map. The team-after block now says declines above the cutoff and approvals below it, and the compliance role says the map from model drivers to decline reasons.

Asked whether one loan product can pilot first and what it is worth. The first test step now records numbers for one loan product, matching the shadow run in the recipes. The pricing step already turns the lift into dollars at the cutoff.

The head of lending checked each role against the exam manuals. The chief credit officer now owns the cutoffs and override authority, and each override names the approving officer. The validator role now says a small lender can use an outside reviewer but still owns the result.
